St. Albans.wildlife_intro:
St. Albans blends a small city's wildlife with farm and bay country. In the city, raccoons, squirrels, and bats work the historic housing, rats appear around older commercial and rail-side blocks, and skunks are a spring fixture under porches. Out in the town, St. Albans Bay camps draw raccoons and bats, and the dairy farms draw the full barn cast — raccoons, skunks, rats, and woodchucks in the fields.

Opossums are established in the Champlain Valley, and St. Albans is well within their range, so they are regular visitors here. Fall is the proofing season before a cold Lake Champlain winter, spring brings denning animals, and bat exclusion is timed for spring or late August through fall with one-way doors — winter for proofing, never colony work while pups cannot fly. Our crew covers both the city streets and the bay shore, so call us wherever in St. Albans you are.

faqs.q: Why do I see opossums in St. Albans more than in the Northeast Kingdom?
faqs.a: Opossums are established in the milder Champlain and Connecticut River valleys but remain scarce in the colder Northeast Kingdom. St. Albans sits in the Champlain Valley, so food and den sites under decks and in garages suit them here. They are usually passing through, but our crew can remove one that has settled in and close the access.

Enosburg Falls is dairy country, and its wildlife calls start in the barn: raccoons, skunks, and rats in feed rooms, bats in big barn lofts and village attics, and woodchucks under sheds and along field edges everywhere. In the village, squirrels and raccoons work the older homes above the falls, and mice are a hard fall problem in houses surrounded by fields and woods on every side.

Our crew times Enosburg work to the farm year — proofing barns and homes in fall before the cold, dealing with denning raccoons and skunks in spring, and fitting bat exclusions to the legal and humane windows in spring and late August through fall. Winter proofing is done while colonies are away, and no bat work seals in flightless pups. Vermont requires a valid trapping license for compensated trapping, and our crew works under one — ask us about it when you call.

faqs.q: Why are rats a problem on Enosburg dairy farms?

Lasting control combines securing feed where possible, trapping the rats present, and closing the worst access points — our crew handles that whole sequence. Poison alone rarely solves a farm rat problem and puts other animals at risk.

Out of the village, porcupines damage camps and outbuildings in the border woods, woodchucks work the river farms, and skunks are a spring constant under porches across town.

Because Vermont prohibits relocating furbearers, our crew will lay out the lawful removal options for raccoons and skunks plainly when you call.

faqs.q: Can a raccoon in my Richford chimney be a mother with young?
faqs.a: In spring and early summer, very often yes — chimneys are a favorite den, warm and safe from predators. Our crew checks for young before any removal, reunites or handles the family lawfully and humanely, and then caps and proofs the chimney so it does not happen again next spring. Never light a fire to drive one out; call us instead.
